reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Rare disaccharidase deficiency, attributed to reduced brush-border trehalase encoded by TREH
Trehalose is found chiefly in mushrooms and some processed foods, so symptoms follow their ingestion
Presents with osmotic diarrhoea, bloating, cramping and flatulence after trehalose-containing meals
The mechanism is failure to hydrolyse trehalose to glucose, leaving an osmotically active, fermentable sugar in the lumen
Symptoms are dose-dependent and resolve on avoidance of trehalose-rich foods
Diagnosis can be supported by low trehalase activity on duodenal disaccharidase assay and by a trehalose breath test
The condition is often under-recognised and may be mistaken for a functional bowel disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Trehalase deficiency is an osmotic malabsorption disorder of the intestinal brush border. Trehalase, encoded by TREH, hydrolyses the disaccharide trehalose into two glucose molecules for absorption. When trehalase activity is deficient, ingested trehalose, present mainly in mushrooms and certain processed foods, is not digested and remains in the lumen. The unabsorbed sugar draws water osmotically into the bowel and is fermented by colonic bacteria into gas and short-chain acids, producing diarrhoea, bloating and flatulence after trehalose-containing meals. Because exposure is intermittent and food-specific, symptoms occur only after relevant ingestions.
additionalDifferentials: Functional gastrointestinal disorders and irritable bowel syndrome
Other food intolerances and FODMAP sensitivity
additionalInvestigations: Dietary history correlating symptoms with mushroom or trehalose-containing food intake
Duodenal biopsy with disaccharidase assay including trehalase activity
Stool pH and reducing substances after a trehalose challenge
Molecular assessment of TREH where available and trial of trehalose elimination
redFlags: Dehydration during acute diarrhoeal episodes, particularly in young children
Weight loss or failure to thrive suggesting a broader malabsorptive process
Persistent symptoms despite trehalose avoidance indicating another diagnosis
New alarm features prompting evaluation for mucosal disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent, as symptoms are entirely controlled by avoiding trehalose-rich foods and there are no systemic consequences. Recognition prevents unnecessary investigation for functional disorders.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent post-meal symptoms to a functional disorder without taking a focused dietary history
Overlooking trehalose as a hidden ingredient in some processed foods
Failing to include trehalase in the disaccharidase assay panel
Assuming symptoms reflect a more common sugar intolerance without confirmatory testing
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Dietary elimination of trehalose-rich foods, chiefly mushrooms and certain processed foods, as the definitive and curative measure
Dietitian support to identify hidden dietary sources of trehalose and maintain nutritional adequacy
Educate that symptoms are dose-dependent and resolve fully on avoidance, so strict blanket restriction is not always required
Confirm the diagnosis with a duodenal disaccharidase assay showing low trehalase activity or a trehalose breath test, preventing unnecessary investigation for functional bowel disease
Reassure that the condition is benign with no systemic consequences once relevant foods are avoided
